Phase I first-in-human.requires: no prior human exposure, dose escalation design
Phase I first-in-human.provides: tens of participants, safety focus only, no efficacy power

Phase II efficacy signal.provides: hundreds of participants, signal detection, not confirmatory

Phase III confirmatory.requires: a defined dose and a demonstrated signal
Phase III confirmatory.provides: thousands of participants, regulatory-grade evidence, years of follow-up

Post-marketing surveillance.requires: an approved licensed product already in use
Post-marketing surveillance.provides: very large populations, real-world conditions, no randomisation

Placebo.requires: withholding active treatment to be ethically acceptable
Placebo.provides: clean comparison, unacceptable where effective therapy exists

Active comparator.requires: an existing approved therapy to compare against
Active comparator.provides: relative efficacy evidence, larger sample sizes needed

No control single arm.requires: an outcome so poor that historical comparison suffices
No control single arm.provides: fast small studies, no causal attribution

Healthy volunteers.requires: no disease and no prospect of benefit
Healthy volunteers.provides: clean pharmacokinetics, no efficacy measurement possible, tolerance only for low-risk agents

Treatment-naive patients.provides: uncontaminated response measurement, ethical obligation to offer standard care

Refractory patients.provides: no effective alternative exists, ethically permits single-arm designs, poor prognosis

Paediatric patients.requires: prior adult safety data and specific regulatory authorisation
Paediatric patients.provides: age-appropriate formulation and endpoints, heightened ethical scrutiny

Safety and tolerability.provides: measurable in any population, no efficacy claim

Biomarker response.provides: fast readout, surrogate not outcome, insufficient for approval alone

Overall survival.requires: years of follow-up and a fatal condition
Overall survival.provides: definitive regulatory endpoint, slow and expensive

Patient-reported outcome.provides: quality of life evidence, unmeasurable in healthy volunteers

_v1_notes.TRIAL PHASE|CONTROL ARM: Phase I is dose escalation in tens of people; placebo, active comparator and standard of care are all N because there is no efficacy comparison being made. Phase III single-arm is N: confirmatory evidence requires a control. Post-marketing has no randomisation, so placebo and active comparator are N; standard of care as an observational comparison is Y.
_v1_notes.TRIAL PHASE|POPULATION: healthy volunteers are N beyond Phase I - later phases measure efficacy, which requires disease. Refractory and paediatric are N in Phase I: neither population is exposed to a first-in-human agent. Treatment-naive is Y throughout.
_v1_notes.TRIAL PHASE|PRIMARY ENDPOINT: Phase I supports safety only. Biomarker response is N in Phase III and post-marketing, where surrogates do not suffice. Overall survival is N in Phase II, which lacks the follow-up and power.
_v1_notes.CONTROL ARM|POPULATION: placebo is N in treatment-naive, refractory and paediatric patients - withholding treatment where therapy exists or where the patient is a child is not acceptable; it is Y only in healthy volunteers. Active comparator and standard of care are both N in healthy volunteers, who have nothing to treat. Single arm is Y only in refractory patients, where no alternative exists.
_v1_notes.CONTROL ARM|PRIMARY ENDPOINT: single arm x overall survival is N: attributing a survival difference requires a control.
_v1_notes.POPULATION|PRIMARY ENDPOINT: healthy volunteers cannot yield overall survival or a patient-reported outcome - there is no disease to survive or to report on.
